messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Parole Officer
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 67

He is a 34-year-old African man who works as a parole officer and comes to therapy carrying himself with the controlled, observant manner that has served him well in his job. He describes that for years he was the one other people depended on to stay calm under pressure, to notice risk before it escalates, to speak firmly without losing his footing. That sense of steadiness changed after the relationship he had thought was becoming a safe place instead became the setting for repeated physical abuse.

He first met his partner as someone warm, attentive, and easy to trust. In the beginning, he feels proud of how open he becomes, because he does not usually let people in quickly. He is used to managing himself, keeping emotions contained, and presenting as capable. Over time, though, the relationship turns volatile. Arguments that begin with jealousy, accusations, or small frustrations can shift without warning. At first, he tries to reason with her, then tries to de-escalate, then tries to avoid saying anything that might set her off. He finds himself monitoring her moods the way he monitors clients in his work—watching for a change in tone, a tightening jaw, the moment a conversation is about to become dangerous.

The first time she hits him, he is stunned more by the betrayal than the pain. He remembers the sharpness of the moment, how quickly the situation moves from disbelief to instinct, and how he tells himself it will never happen again. But it does. The abuse becomes cyclical: a blow, an apology, a period of calm, then tension that builds again. He starts to shrink his life to fit around her volatility. He avoids naming his injuries. He cancels plans with friends. He becomes skilled at covering marks, arriving at work with a careful expression and a story about bumping into a door or training too hard at the gym. He is ashamed that he cannot simply leave, and ashamed that a man in his position—someone who works with people on probation, someone who is expected to understand control and consequences—can feel so powerless in his own home.

He begins to live as if danger is always close by. In crowded places he tracks exits automatically. He startles when a door slams or someone reaches toward him too quickly. At home, his body braces before he even knows why. Sleep becomes light and fragmented. He wakes tense, listening for footsteps, the sound of keys, the shift in her breathing that would mean an argument is coming. During the day, he tries to stay focused at work, but his mind drifts to whether he left her in a bad mood, whether he said the wrong thing, whether he will find a text waiting that makes his stomach drop. He becomes more irritable with coworkers and more detached with family, not because he wants distance, but because he feels exhausted by the effort of staying composed.

His work as a parole officer starts to feel different. He remains competent, but he notices that he is less patient with deception and more sensitive to signs of aggression. A raised voice in an office meeting can leave him sweating and distracted. He sometimes feels his chest tighten when he is interviewing a client who paces the room or leans in too close. He worries that others will notice how often he scans for threat. Even simple moments become difficult: hearing laughter in another room can make him think, for an instant, that something is about to break. He finds himself replaying scenes from the relationship without meaning to, especially at night, and then feeling angry at himself for being unable to shut them off.

Now, though he is still in a relationship, he speaks of living with a constant internal alertness that never fully turns off. He is trying to make sense of how love became fear and why he stayed as long as he did. He does not describe himself as broken, but as someone whose body learned too well that home could become unsafe. In session, he speaks carefully at first, then with more feeling as the story unfolds. He is protective of his dignity, and beneath that protection there is grief—for the version of himself who felt secure, for the trust he extended, and for the way violence has altered the ordinary rhythms of his days.
